articles.title: A DIY builder has turned more than 1,000 discarded laptop batteries into a home battery bank kept in a separate shed, storing solar power from his panels that can even run his washing machine
articles.summary: A DIY enthusiast in France has found a way to give discarded laptop batteries a second life by turning them into a large home energy storage system.
articles.body: A DIY enthusiast in France has found a way to give discarded laptop batteries a second life by turning them into a large home energy storage system. Using more than 1,000 salvaged laptop batteries, the builder has assembled a battery bank inside a separate shed, where it stores electricity generated by his solar panels. The unique setup has gradually expanded over the years and can now supply power to household appliances, including a washing machine, according to reports detailing the project.Discarded laptop batteries became a home energy storage bankThe project was started by a DIY builder known online as Glubux, who began documenting his efforts on the Second Life Storage forum in November 2016. According to Interesting Engineering, he initially had around 650 used laptop batteries, a small rooftop solar installation and an old forklift battery that he used to store electricity.Rather than throwing away the laptop batteries, Glubux realised that individual cells inside them could still hold electricity even when the complete battery pack had stopped working. Laptop battery packs contain several individual cells, and the failure of just one can sometimes make the entire pack unusable.This provided an opportunity to recover the working cells and reuse them for a different purpose. According to Futura-Sciences, Glubux began opening the discarded battery packs, testing their individual lithium-ion cells and separating those that could still be used.The builder's approach was not simply to connect every recovered cell together. He tested the cells individually, removed weaker or damaged ones and grouped the usable units according to their capacity. The remaining cells were assembled into larger battery blocks, which eventually became the foundation of his home energy storage system.What powers this unique battery bankThe storage system has grown considerably since its early days. Interesting Engineering reported that Glubux initially had around 1.4 kilowatts of rooftop solar panels, an old 24-volt forklift battery and a 3-kilovolt-ampere inverter.As the project developed, he expanded the solar installation by adding 24 more panels, each rated at 440 watts. This brought the total solar generation capacity to nearly 10.6 kilowatts, giving the system a considerably larger supply of electricity to store.Ecoportal reported that the battery bank's storage capacity increased from approximately 7 kilowatt-hours at the beginning to around 56 kilowatt-hours over the years. This expansion allowed the builder to store considerably more electricity generated during daylight hours and use it later when sunlight was unavailable.The battery system operates at 24 volts and supplies electricity through a 3-kilovolt-ampere converter. As reported by TheCoolDown, the arrangement can power household appliances, with Glubux even claiming that his washing machine runs using electricity supplied by the homemade battery bank.The setup also includes the original forklift battery, which remained part of the system as it expanded. Interesting Engineering reported that it continued to help manage the electricity supply while the recycled laptop cells handled the growing storage requirements.The builder keeps the batteries in a separate shedOne of the most distinctive features of the project is the location of the battery bank. Instead of installing hundreds of recycled lithium-ion cells inside his home, Glubux built a separate shed to accommodate the storage equipment.According to TheCoolDown, the shed is located approximately 50 metres from his house. It contains the battery racks, charge controllers and inverters that manage the electricity generated by the solar panels.The recovered cells are arranged in holders and connected together in organised groups. The electricity travels from the shed towards the house, where it is converted into a supply that can be used by ordinary household appliances.Keeping the equipment away from the main living space also separates the battery installation from the areas where the family spends its time.How long has the recycled battery system continued workingThe project's longevity is another reason it has attracted attention. Glubux began sharing updates in 2016, and reports published nearly a decade later describe the system as continuing to operate.Interesting Engineering reported in November 2025 that the installation had been running for 8 years without a major failure. The report also stated that no individual battery cell had failed during that period.However, these performance figures come from the builder's own accounts and project updates. Futura-Sciences highlighted that the reported 56-kilowatt-hour capacity has not been independently verified and that battery performance can decline over time.The safety risks behind reusing old lithium-ion batteriesReusing discarded laptop batteries is not a straightforward household project, particularly because lithium-ion cells can become dangerous if they are damaged, incorrectly connected or poorly managed.Futura-Sciences warned that old cells can develop internal damage and chemical deterioration, potentially leading to short circuits, overheating and fires. Differences in the age, condition and electrical resistance of individual cells can also create imbalances when they are connected in a large storage system.A damaged or overcharged cell can trigger a process known as ‘thermal runaway,’ in which rising temperatures can cause further overheating.You use AI every day. articles.title: Who is Kilmar Abrego Garcia? Salvadoran man whose deportation sparked legal battle moves to Spain
articles.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran man whose deportation ignited a legal battle with the Trump administration, has moved to Spain. His case highlights immigration policy complexities and human rights concerns.
articles.body: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national whose deportation to El Salvador triggered a major legal battle with the Trump administration, has arrived in Spain after voluntarily leaving the United States.The 31-year-old landed in Madrid on Wednesday morning on a commercial flight, accompanied by his American wife and lawyer, according to CNN. His attorney, Chris Newman, told the outlet that Garcia entered Spain on a tourist visa that allows him to stay for up to 90 days.His departure comes after months of legal disputes over the US government's attempts to deport him to another country. The case also brought national attention to the Trump administration's immigration crackdown after officials mistakenly sent him to a prison in El Salvador despite an earlier court order preventing his removal there.Garcia had been living in Maryland before his arrest in March last year. He entered the United States without legal authorisation around 2011 and later built a life there with his family, according to the broadcast media.His immigration case took a significant turn in 2019 when an immigration judge ruled that he could not be sent back to El Salvador. The decision followed concerns that a gang had threatened to kill him because of his family's pupusa business.Despite the ruling, US authorities arrested Garcia in March last year and deported him to El Salvador. He was subsequently held at the country's Terrorism Confinement Centre, commonly known as Cecot, a high-security prison.The Trump administration later acknowledged in court documents that his deportation had happened because of an administrative error. A federal judge ordered officials to work towards bringing him back to the United States, but the government resisted for several months.Garcia eventually returned to the US in June last year after the administration reached an arrangement with the Salvadoran government. However, his legal troubles did not end there.After his return, authorities arrested him on human smuggling charges linked to an earlier case. Garcia denied the allegations, and a federal judge dismissed the charges in May, citing what the court described as a "tainted investigation" by Attorney General Todd Blanche.The government challenged that decision and continued pursuing his deportation to another country. Officials considered several destinations in Africa, including Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and Liberia, according to AP.Garcia had expressed a preference for Costa Rica, which had indicated it was willing to provide him with some form of legal status. However, conditions imposed by the judge who dismissed his criminal charges prevented him from voluntarily moving there.An AP report also cited a March memo by former acting ICE director Todd Lyons, who argued against sending Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica, describing the move as "prejudicial to the United States". Lyons instead supported deporting him to Liberia.The Department of Homeland Security announced Garcia's departure from the US on Tuesday. Advocacy group We Are CASA, which supported him and his family throughout the legal battle, also confirmed the development, saying he had "walked out of the United States a free man".Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents removed his ankle monitor at Washington Dulles International Airport before he boarded his flight.Political reaction after Abrego Garcia leaves USMaryland Senator Chris Van Hollen welcomed his departure, recalling his visit to El Salvador last year, where he met Abrego Garcia while he was being held at the Cecot prison.In a statement posted on Tuesday, Van Hollen said the Trump administration had once sought to leave Abrego Garcia imprisoned in El Salvador, but he was now travelling to a country of his choice.He also said he was relieved that Abrego Garcia would be free from what he described as the administration's continued persecution.The DHS, however, criticised his decision to move to Spain. In a social media post, the department described him as a "criminal illegal alien" and attacked Spain's immigration policies, calling the country a destination for illegal migration.Abrego Garcia's case unfolded against the backdrop of Trump's wider immigration crackdown, which began shortly after he returned to the White House in January 2025. The president had pledged to deport one million people during his first year back in office.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Meta's top executives in India met Congress leaders on Tuesday amid escalating protests over alleged political bias and restrictions on
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Meta's top executives in India met Congress leaders on Tuesday amid escalating protests over alleged political bias and restrictions on opposition voices on its platforms.The meeting came as the party stepped up its campaign against the social media giant, accusing it of favouring the ruling BJP.Meta executives Aman Jain and Natasha Jog represented the company at the meeting at Congress headquarters, four people familiar with the matter told Reuters. It was the first direct engagement between the two sides since the Congress's youth wing began protests on Friday.During the meeting, Meta executives raised concerns over protests targeting the company's offices and posters depicting CEO Mark Zuckerberg in an RSS-style uniform.Congress, meanwhile, flagged increasing restrictions on its leaders' accounts and posts, alleging that Meta favoured Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling BJP, three people familiar with the discussions told Reuters.The meeting followed protests launched by the Congress's youth wing on Friday over alleged restrictions on opposition leaders' social media accounts.The Youth Congress has demanded that Meta restore accounts taken down on government orders and explain how its algorithms decide which political posts are restricted.Meta made no commitments to Congress during the meeting. Its executives maintained that the company followed Indian laws and remained neutral towards all political parties, one person with direct knowledge of the discussions said.Protesters also clashed with police near Meta's offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram. The demonstrations later spread to Delhi, Kolkata, Patna and Bengaluru, where posters depicting Zuckerberg in the traditional RSS uniform appeared.The protests have also brought renewed attention to the scale of content restrictions imposed by Meta in India. The company restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts under local laws in the first half of 2026, compared with around 70,000 during the entire year in 2025, according to company disclosures cited by Reuters.Meta has attributed the increase to amendments to India's IT rules, which require platforms to remove content more quickly and proactively. articles.title: Two sons say their father's 12 gold coins, allegedly worth $400,000, were taken by a stepbrother and sold through an auction house; a November 20 federal judge allowed their lawsuit against the auctioneer to proceed
articles.summary: Two brothers are pursuing a lawsuit against an auction house over 12 gold coins they say were taken from their late father's collection and sold without
articles.body: Two brothers are pursuing a lawsuit against an auction house over 12 gold coins they say were taken from their late father's collection and sold without their knowledge. They allege that their stepbrother handed the coins to Scotsman Coin & Jewelry Inc., which later sold them to buyers at an auction in July 2021.The coins, comprising $10 and $20 Carson City gold pieces, are estimated to be worth around $400,000. The brothers, Bradley Middleton and Christopher Middleton, say their father had specifically left these coins to them in his will.According to case details on Justia, the dispute came to light while the family was settling their father's estate. The brothers say they discovered that the coins were missing while checking his collection and preparing an inventory of his assets. They subsequently brought a claim against the auction house, alleging that it had wrongfully sold property belonging to them.The case has now cleared an important hurdle. On November 20, a federal judge refused to dismiss the brothers' lawsuit against the auctioneer. The decision allows the case to proceed.Family inheritance dispute preceded discoveryThe brothers' father, Benjamin Middleton, died on January 8, 2021. He was survived by his wife, Kathleen Middleton, and three adult sons, including Bradley and Christopher. Joseph Canfield, Kathleen's son from an earlier relationship, was Benjamin's stepson.Benjamin had made arrangements for his coin and precious metals collection through his will and subsequent amendments. A document signed in 2013 specifically excluded Canfield from inheriting anything from his estate. It also set out how certain coins were to be distributed among the family members.Following Benjamin's death, disagreements arose over his will and the division of his collection. The family eventually reached a settlement through mediation in June 2021. Under the agreement, Kathleen accepted the distribution set out in her husband's will and agreed that the coins listed for Bradley and Christopher should go to them.The agreement also allowed the brothers to examine their father's collection and search his former home in Portland, Oregon, for the coins mentioned in the will. Benjamin had reportedly hidden coins in different places around the property, making a search necessary.The brothers carried out the inspection on July 16, 2021. A court approved their family settlement the following month, and Bradley was appointed to manage the estate.Missing coins traced to auction houseWhile preparing the estate's inventory, Bradley discovered that 12 coins intended for him and Christopher had been sold. He found this on September 24, 2021, according to the court order.The coins had already appeared in Scotsman Coin & Jewelry's Midwest Summer Sale, held on July 23, 2021. They were listed under the name Sheffield Collection across several lots and were sold to buyers whose identities were not specified in the court document.The brothers allege that Canfield took the coins sometime after Benjamin's death and arranged for their sale through the auction house. They claim the transaction took place without their knowledge, despite the coins having been left to them under their father's will.Their lawsuit also alleges that the auction house advanced money to Canfield in anticipation of the auction. The brothers argue that the auctioneer's involvement in handling and selling the coins deprived them of property they were legally entitled to receive. They are seeking $400,000 in damages, based on their estimate of the coins' value.Judge rejects auction house's request to dismiss caseScotsman Coin & Jewelry sought dismissal of the lawsuit, arguing that the brothers had not made a sufficient case against the company. It also contended that Canfield and their father's estate should have been included in the proceedings. US District Judge Henry Edward Autrey rejected the request on November 20.The judge found that the brothers had presented sufficient grounds to pursue their claim. Their lawsuit identifies them as the intended owners of the coins under the will and the subsequent family settlement. It also alleges that the auction house handled and sold the coins after receiving them from Canfield.The auction house further argued that the case could not proceed without Canfield, given his alleged role in the transaction. The judge disagreed, noting that a lawsuit against one party accused of contributing to a wrongful act does not always require every other alleged participant to be included.The court also found no reason to dismiss the case because the estate had not been named as a party. The estate had transferred its interest in the claims to Bradley and Christopher, the judge noted.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Viral Georgia Tech couple caught arguing on ESPN during football game reveals what really happened; 'It was completely insignificant', and they did not break up
articles.summary: A young couple whose apparently heated argument during a college football game was analysed live by ESPN commentators has revealed what was actually
articles.body: A young couple whose apparently heated argument during a college football game was analysed live by ESPN commentators has revealed what was actually happening between them, putting an end to speculation that viewers had witnessed a breakup. Georgia Tech students Tallulah Wall and Braden Flournoy went viral for their animated argument but they have now revealed that it was nothing serious but just a minor disagreement.Both are 21-year-old fourth-year students at Georgia Tech. Wall is studying mechanical engineering, while Flournoy is a computer science major.The couple, who appeared on NBC's Today show on November 24, insisted there was never any question of ending their relationship. "Honestly, it was completely insignificant," Flournoy said, explaining that the conversation had been blown out of proportion by the camera angles and the commentary. "It was more miscommunication than anything," he added.Wall said there had been considerable miscommunication between them. But then they decided to take a break from bickering and watch the match though their team was losing. The incident took place on November 21, when ESPN cameras focused on the couple sitting in the stands during Georgia Tech's home game against Wake Forest in Atlanta.The pair appeared to be having an intense conversation, with their facial expressions and body language attracting the attention of the broadcast team. ESPN analyst Jesse Palmer began offering his interpretation of what was happening. "He is locked in. He is holding her to court right now. He wants an answer. They are in each other's personal space. He's not happy with whatever she just told him," Palmer said as the cameras showed the couple.Play-by-play announcer Joe Tessitore encouraged Palmer to break down the interaction, and the analyst even used the broadcast's telestrator to illustrate his observations. The cameras returned to the couple a little later, this time showing them kissing after apparently making up. "That's good news," Palmer said.Tessitore added, "Embrace the love, America," while Palmer jokingly advised them to "get a room".The clip quickly went viral with social media users jumping in to guess what happened between them during the game. Some of their friends were shocked as they did not even know that they were dating.Wall and Flournoy said they had been together for two months and one week but had largely kept their relationship private."A lot of our friends actually had no idea we were dating until that happened," Flournoy said.Wall recalled receiving messages from people who had seen them on television. Some were asking whether she had a boyfriend, while others were simply informing her that the couple had appeared on the ESPN broadcast. They said they first realised they had become an internet sensation when a stadium employee showed them footage of their interaction. articles.title: Two 18-year-olds in upstate New York turned a high school Spanish class project into a junk removal business, and a year later, they are using their profit to give away 50 free Thanksgiving turkeys
articles.summary: One person's trash is another's treasure, and for two teens from Hudson, that idea became a business.
articles.body: One person's trash is another's treasure, and for two teens from Hudson, that idea became a business. Jean-Edmond Molnar and Jasper Pappas built Junk Busters by hauling away other people's cast-offs, and now that same work is paying for something they can give back to their community. The 18-year-olds planned to give away 50 free Thanksgiving turkeys at Henry Hudson Riverfront Park, funded by what they earned on the job, according to a report by the Daily Gazette.A Spanish project turned into a solid businessJean-Edmond Molnar, of Hudson, and Jasper Pappas, of Philmont, did not set out to start a company. They were assigned a project in their high school Spanish class, and it grew into a real business that now serves customers across the Hudson Valley. Fresh out of high school, the teens decided they did not want to wait around for someone to give them a job. So they founded Junk Busters during the 2025 holiday season. The initial months involved a great deal of hard work. They spent long days knocking on doors and posting in local Facebook groups to find customers. Their truck had a hole in the floor, and rope served as the door handles.But a job in New Lebanon changed things. While clearing out a property, the partners spotted a Ford Ranger pickup that the client might be willing to sell. The truck had belonged to her late husband, and she planned to scrap it. Instead, she gave it to the young business owners on the spot. The teenagers say that very gift changed the course of their business. They only began making progress from that point onwards.Much of what the company hauls away is still useful. The teens repair what they can and donate the rest, including clothing, toys and furniture, to Goodwill and The Second Show, a thrift store in Hudson. Molnar summed up the approach: "We try not to just throw everything in a landfill."Free Thanksgiving turkeys for the communityThe teens know how a helping hand from that woman in New Lebanon changed their lives. Now that their business is successful, they want to give something back to the community. This holiday season, the teen entrepreneurs planned a turkey giveaway. They gave away 50 free turkeys at Henry Hudson Riverfront Park on Saturday at 2.30 pm. The money comes from the profits of their business. "This is all money that we made from junk jobs locally in the community, and we're just repurposing that money into something that actually helps everyone," Jasper Pappas told the paper.But why Thanksgiving turkeys? As the holiday approaches, most families are planning their Thanksgiving celebrations, but for some, the cost of a turkey can make it difficult to enjoy the traditional holiday meal. The teens want to spread some holiday cheer. "Thanksgiving turkeys cost a lot for a family, and I was always grateful for my family being able to afford that. Now that we've grown our business, just being able to provide that experience and help bring people together, like our families were brought together, is really important for us," Pappas added.Thanksgiving falls on 26 November, and turkey is a traditional centrepiece of the holiday meal, but its rising cost can put additional pressure on families preparing for the celebration. Thanksgiving dinner is getting more expensive, and turkey is one of the reasons. Prices for turkey and potatoes, the holiday's two marquee staples, have jumped since last year, Reuters reported. The wholesale price of frozen turkeys rose by 12% from last year, reaching a record $2 per pound as of 9 November, according to commodity data firm Expana.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2005, Washington’s Puyallup Tribe began a salmon hatchery programme that initially saw just a few hundred fish return; in 2026, more than 6,300 Chinook and 6,893 coho have returned
articles.summary: A salmon hatchery programme started with a few hundred returning fish in Washington state has grown into an operation recording thousands of salmon every
articles.body: A salmon hatchery programme started with a few hundred returning fish in Washington state has grown into an operation recording thousands of salmon every year. The Puyallup Tribe's Clarks Creek Salmon Hatchery recorded more than 6,300 Chinook salmon and 6,893 coho salmon returning in 2026, marking a record season for Chinook.The programme began in 2005 and has gradually expanded through improvements to the hatchery and work to improve fish habitats, according to the tribe's website. The increase in returning salmon has also changed what the facility can do. It now collects its own eggs every year instead of depending on supplies from other hatcheries to sustain its operations.The progress is also allowing the tribe to support other fisheries programmes. In October, the Puyallup Tribal Fisheries Department supplied coho salmon eggs to the Suquamish Tribe, which was struggling with a shortage. It was the first time eggs from the Clarks Creek facility had been transferred to another tribe and watershed.Meanwhile, another round of construction is underway at Clarks Creek. The new facilities are designed to increase the number of fish the hatchery can handle and reduce the effort required from workers during collection. They are expected to become operational in June 2027.A record season for ChinookThe latest returns represent a significant change from the hatchery's early years. When the programme started in 2005, only a few hundred salmon made their way back. The numbers have increased gradually since then.By the end of October, Chinook returns had exceeded 6,300, setting a new record for the hatchery. Coho numbers had also reached 6,893. Of the returning coho, 5,981 adult fish had been moved into local streams.Blake Smith, fisheries enhancement chief for the Puyallup Tribe, attributed the improvement to two decades of work on the hatchery programme and fish habitats.The facility's growing capacity has also reduced its dependence on outside supplies. The programme initially received eggs from the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife and Voight's Creek Hatchery. It has now reached a stage where it can collect the eggs needed for its operations each year.The tribe is continuing to upgrade the facility to maintain the programme for future generations. The latest construction project focuses on broodstock ponds, where returning adult fish can be handled for breeding purposes.How young salmon make their way backThe hatchery programme follows the natural life cycle of salmon, with the facility helping raise young fish before they are released into the wild.Chinook, coho and chub salmon begin their lives in freshwater streams. They later move to the ocean and return to freshwater locations to reproduce. Their return periods differ: Chinook arrive between July and October, coho between September and November, and chub between November and December.When adult fish return, hatchery workers collect eggs from females and milt, which contains sperm, from males. These are used for fertilisation, with incubation beginning in late autumn or early winter.For Chinook, hatching takes approximately 85 days. The newly hatched fish are called alevins and initially have yolk sacs attached to their bodies. They depend on these sacs for nourishment. After the sacs are used up, the young fish are called fry and are transferred to artificial channels known as raceways.They continue developing there before reaching the smolt or yearling stages. In February or March, hatchery workers mark them using coded wire tags and fin clipping. These markings help identify the fish and collect information about their movement.The young salmon are released into the wild during spring, when they begin travelling towards the ocean. Fish raised at Clarks Creek are mainly caught by tribal fishers near Vancouver Island and the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Some have been found as far south as Brookings in Oregon.New systems to reduce work at the hatcheryThe next phase of development at Clarks Creek is aimed at changing how workers handle returning fish. At present, employees have to catch the fish individually using nets. The work is physically demanding and takes considerable time. The planned equipment will automate several parts of the process and allow staff to spend less time handling individual fish.The new broodstock ponds will include automatic fish crowders. These systems use moving barriers to direct fish towards a smaller collection area. An electro-anesthesia system will temporarily stun fish, making them easier to collect.Another addition will be an Archimedes screw, a mechanism that moves fish upwards towards the water surface or collection containers.The changes are expected to increase the number of fish that can be processed while reducing stress on them. Staff will also be able to carry out collection work without entering the water.The ponds will have automatic fish-counting systems as well. An overhead structure and sprinklers are planned to limit exposure to sunlight and help control water temperatures.The new facilities are scheduled to open in June 2027, shortly before Chinook begin returning to the hatchery in July.Coho eggs help another tribe address shortageThe Puyallup Tribe's growing coho supply has also enabled it to assist the Suquamish Tribe with its hatchery programme.Suquamish fisheries representatives visited Clarks Creek on October 27 to collect eggs after facing a shortage of coho. The tribe needed 60,000 eggs for its programme.The shortfall followed a decision to remove some eggs during a process intended to ensure healthier fish for reintroduction. Suquamish had also recorded fewer returning Chinook than expected. This left additional space in its hatchery, which the tribe decided to use for raising more coho.The eggs supplied by Puyallup will help the Suquamish programme work towards releasing up to 480,000 healthy, delayed-release coho smolts through its Agate Pass net pen programme. The fish are intended to support tribal fisheries as well as recreational and commercial fishing.The transfer followed a review process involving the managers of the coho fishery. The eggs were kept separate from other fish and the surrounding environment while health checks were pending. Samples were being examined for viruses and bacteria, and any eggs found to be infected would have to be destroyed.The transfer also reflects cooperation between tribes in Washington state on fisheries and wildlife management. Such arrangements developed further after the 1974 Boldt Decision required state and federal authorities to recognise tribal access to ancestral fisheries.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Missouri couple sought permission for 12 rooftop solar panels, but their homeowners association demanded five neighbours’ consent and rejected the plan; an appeals court has now overturned the HOA’s legal-fee award
articles.summary: A Missouri couple who wanted to put 12 solar panels on their roof faced pushback from their homeowners association (HOA).
articles.body: A Missouri couple who wanted to put 12 solar panels on their roof faced pushback from their homeowners association (HOA). The group demanded signed approval from five neighbours before turning down their request. The fight went to an appeals court, which has now cancelled an order forcing the homeowners to pay the association's legal bills.The Missouri Court of Appeals for the Western District sided with Laurie McGuire and her co-owner in a ruling issued on 24 November 2026. The court said the Thousand Oaks Homes Association had no legal right to get its legal costs paid because the couple had not broken any neighbourhood property rules. The judges also rejected the HOA's claim that going to court to challenge solar panel limits counted as breaking the homeowners' agreement, explaining that residents have a right to ask judges to clarify their rights without automatically being treated like rule-breakers.The case focused on Missouri's solar energy law, which stops homeowners associations from blocking rooftop solar panels with strict rules. It also asked whether an HOA can make residents pay its legal fees just for questioning how community rules are applied.The solar panel application that started the disputeAccording to the court's decision, the homeowners are a married couple living in the Thousand Oaks subdivision in Parkville, Missouri. As HOA members, they must follow its Declaration of Covenants and Restrictions, a document listing the property rules for the neighbourhood. In January 2023, the couple applied to put 12 solar panels on their roof. Three months later, the association sent a letter rejecting the plan for two reasons. First, the couple did not include five neighbour consent forms required by the Architectural Control Committee Policy. Second, the 12 panels would be visible from the street. The homeowners did not send in a new design. Instead, they took the association to court, arguing that parts of its property rules and architectural policy went against Missouri's solar energy law, Section 442.404.3. They asked the court to declare those rules unlawful and stop the association from using them against their home.Missouri law protects rooftop solar installationsMissouri's solar energy law was at the heart of the couple's case. According to the Revisor of Statutes, Section 442.404.3 of the Revised Statutes of Missouri states that property rules and similar agreements cannot ban or effectively stop homeowners from putting solar panels or solar collectors on their roofs. The law lets homeowners associations set reasonable rules about where panels go, though those rules cannot block the setup, get in the way of how the panels work, limit their use, raise the cost or make them less efficient.The law covers roofs owned, controlled and maintained by individual homeowners. It does not give associations total power to reject solar panels just because they do not match the look the group wants for a neighbourhood. The homeowners argued that the Thousand Oaks association's demands violated these legal protections and asked for a permanent order stopping the HOA from enforcing those parts of its rules and architectural policy. The association replied in June 2023, asking the circuit court to turn down the couple's claims. It also asked to be paid back for its legal costs and reasonable lawyers' fees under the neighbourhood's property rules. According to the appeals court's account, the HOA filed its own counter-petition asking the court to read the rules in its favour, raising a big question about how far an HOA can go when setting rules for rooftop solar panels when state law already limits them.A separate Supreme Court ruling changes the legal positionWhile this case was in court, another solar panel fight reached the Supreme Court of Missouri. On 23 January 2026, the state's highest court gave its ruling in Eikmeier v. Granite Springs Home Owners Association, Inc., as reported by Justia Law. That case involved homeowners Colleen Eikmeier and William Love, whose HOA had rules against solar panels. The Supreme Court ruled that Missouri's solar energy law covers both older property agreements and new ones. It also decided that a rule banning panels on street-facing roofs cannot be enforced if it hurts the system's cost or efficiency. This ruling mattered to the McGuire case because the Thousand Oaks association had also objected to panels being seen from the street, and the Court of Appeals later noted that the HOA would have lost if that January decision had been used to decide the main issue.HOA's legal-fee claim becomes the main disputeThe McGuire case was first set for a summary judgment hearing in July 2025, though the Platte County Circuit Court decided the case was not ready for a decision yet. By November 2025, both sides told the court they had settled their disagreements, except for who would pay the legal fees. In December 2025, the circuit court looked at the association's request to have its legal bills paid, where the homeowners stated they had not broken any neighbourhood rules and had never received a violation notice, and the HOA's president also spoke during the hearing. In January 2026, the circuit court approved the association's request, ruling that the property rules let the HOA recover legal costs spent defending itself against the couple's lawsuit and filing its own counterclaim. The court also found that filing the lawsuit itself broke community rules because the legal case required enforcing the property agreement. The couple and the association later agreed to drop their remaining claims, but the order to pay legal fees stayed in place, leading the homeowners to appeal.Appeals court rejects the association's argumentThe Missouri Court of Appeals looked at whether the couple's choice to go to court could legally count as breaking the homeowners' agreement. The association pointed to Article VIII, Section 2, of its property declaration, which let the group recover legal costs when taking action against residents who broke or tried to break community rules. However, the appeals court found that the couple had not put up any solar panels and had not broken or tried to break any property rules, and an HOA representative also admitted during a sworn statement that the homeowners had no violations and were in good standing. The representative said: "There is no infraction of a covenant until an infraction occurs. To my knowledge, there are no solar panels on said property; therefore, there are no violations that have occurred."The court also noted that the neighbourhood rules did not say filing a lawsuit to clarify legal rights counted as a violation. It said homeowners cannot fairly be treated as breaking their agreements simply because they used their legal right to ask a court what those agreements mean. The association also claimed the couple's lawsuit was an anticipatory breach of their agreement, a legal term that usually applies when someone clearly shows they plan not to follow a contract. The appeals court turned down that claim, finding no proof the homeowners refused to follow their agreement. Instead, they applied to install solar panels and stopped moving forward after the HOA said no. The judges also pointed to an earlier Missouri appeals case, Hague v. Trustees of Highlands of Chesterfield, which decided an HOA cannot collect legal fees without proving residents broke its property rules.Court overturns legal-fee awardIn its 24 November 2026 ruling, the Missouri Court of Appeals agreed with the homeowners' appeal and overturned the circuit court's decision. The judges decided the HOA's legal-fee rule only applied when homeowners broke or tried to break community rules, meaning the association had no right to collect its legal costs since no rule was broken. The appeals court also pointed out that neither side won the main fight because both agreed to drop their claims, and the final order had just confirmed the earlier legal-fee award rather than deciding the original solar panel disagreement. All three judges, Alok Ahuja, Thomas N. Chapman and Janet Sutton, agreed on the ruling. The decision overturned the win for Thousand Oaks Homes Association and wiped out the legal-fee order against the homeowners, though it did not act as a separate order approving the couple's original 12-panel plan. The ruling was issued by the Missouri Court of Appeals' Western District in Laurie McGuire, et al. v. Thousand Oaks Association, Inc., case number WD88802.You use AI every day. articles.title: US Army detonates 5 tons of bomb chemicals in Iowa despite fears of toxic lead plume
articles.summary: The US Army has conducted a controlled detonation of five tons of lead azide at an Iowa facility, despite environmental concerns over potential lead contamination in the air and water supply.
articles.body: The US Army on Wednesday detonated around five tons of lead azide, the country's entire stockpile of the explosive-making chemical, at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa, despite concerns that the blast could release lead-contaminated dust and expose nearby residents to health risks, the Associated Press reported.The explosion took place at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Video footage recorded from several miles away showed two white plumes rising above the site before quickly disappearing.The controlled detonation involved approximately 68 barrels of lead azide, as per AP. The Army had installed concrete and sand barriers around the bunkers and used ballistic gels and foams to absorb lead particles. Officials had also said that thousands of gallons of water would be used to suppress the dust cloud.The operation had faced opposition from environmental groups and residents concerned about possible effects on air quality, water supplies, farms and animals. Authorities had advised people living within five miles of the facility to prepare for evacuation as a precaution.The Army had initially scheduled the explosion for Friday but postponed it three times following public objections and to allow additional safety preparations. A federal appeals court cleared the way for the operation on Monday, ruling that safeguards adopted by the Environmental Protection Agency were adequate to minimise the spread of lead dust.The decision followed concerns about the condition of the decades-old chemical stockpile. During an inspection in March, workers discovered that the lead azide had partially crystallised, making it more sensitive to friction and cold temperatures and raising the possibility of an uncontrolled explosion.The stockpile had been transferred to the Iowa facility from military bases across the country in 2009. Army officials said alternative disposal methods, including thermal treatment and chemical neutralisation, were considered less safe than a controlled detonation.Major General Eric Shirley, who led the Army operation, had warned that delaying the disposal was no longer a viable option, saying: "Inaction is no longer an option."You use AI every day. articles.title: A former Adidas manager who oversaw its partnership with Beyoncé says she lost her job after reporting racial misconduct at work; an Oregon jury has awarded her $1.23 million in punitive damages
articles.summary: An Oregon jury has ordered Adidas America to pay $1.23 million in punitive damages to a former brand manager who oversaw its partnership with Beyoncé.
articles.body: An Oregon jury has ordered Adidas America to pay $1.23 million in punitive damages to a former brand manager who oversaw its partnership with Beyoncé. The jury found that the sportswear company had subjected her to a racially hostile work environment. The Multnomah County Circuit Court jury delivered its decision on 20 November after an eight-day trial in Portland, according to Courtroom View Network (CVN). Jurors agreed that plaintiff April Burton had faced racial misconduct at work. However, they refused to award her any compensatory damages and cleared Adidas of four other claims, including wrongful termination and whistleblower retaliation. Burton, who is African-American, had sought more than $16 million in total damages. This included $6.2 million for financial and emotional harm, along with $10 million in punitive damages.Origins of the workplace disputeBurton worked at Adidas's Portland office, where she managed the Ivy Park product line, the sportswear collaboration with singer Beyoncé. According to trial reports by Wisevoter and Sporting Goods Intelligence (SGI News), her legal dispute began with incidents dating back to 2022. In April 2022, Burton filed an internal complaint with Adidas human resources. She said a senior colleague had called her "ape" while she was working on the Beyoncé brand. Burton claimed the company did not properly address her concerns. By March 2023, the dispute had reached a meeting with senior company leaders, including Adidas chief executive Bjørn Gulden. After the Ivy Park partnership ended, Burton claimed she was overlooked for a promotion to a director-level position and was instead given a lower-ranking role. She filed her first lawsuit in Multnomah County in September 2024 while she was still working for the company. In February 2025, Adidas placed her on administrative leave and later dismissed her. Burton then changed her lawsuit to add claims that the company had retaliated against her.Adidas defends its internal investigationDuring the trial before Judge Shelly Russell, Adidas lawyers strongly challenged Burton's account of events. Sarah Benedict, a lawyer from Davis Wright Tremaine representing the sportswear company, argued that its leaders had taken her original racial complaint seriously and arranged direct talks with the chief executive. According to CVN's trial report, defence lawyers argued that the nickname Burton mentioned was actually a shortened version of her first name, April, rather than a racial slur. Adidas also argued that Burton's dismissal in February 2025 was not connected to her complaints or lawsuit. Instead, Benedict told jurors that a detailed internal investigation had uncovered complaints from more than a dozen colleagues, including other Black women. They described Burton as difficult to work with and said she often acted in a combative manner. At least three employees had allegedly threatened to leave the company because of workplace tensions involving her."Ms. Burton was let go only after and because of an investigation that substantiated findings of bullying, demeaning comments and a pattern of mistreating her colleagues," Benedict told the court during opening statements, as recorded by CVN. The defence also said human resources staff had tried to arrange several interviews to address tensions within the team. However, Burton allegedly refused to take part or consider whether her own behaviour had contributed to the problems. On her role after the Beyoncé line ended, Adidas said it had tried to keep Ivy Park staff employed without cutting their pay rather than making them redundant. "It wouldn't necessarily be their dream job," Benedict told jurors. "It wasn't an opportunity to pick any job at the company that you wanted."Split verdict and reaction from the companyAfter closing arguments on 19 November, the jury began its discussions and delivered a split decision the following morning. Jurors found Adidas America responsible for maintaining a racially hostile work environment, awarding Burton $1.23 million in punitive damages. However, the jury rejected her claims of unfair treatment at work based on race, gender discrimination, whistleblower retaliation and unpaid wages, according to SGI News. The decision to award no compensatory damages indicated that jurors did not find that Burton had suffered direct financial losses from an unfair dismissal, even though they decided to penalise the company over the workplace environment.In a statement issued to the media after the verdict, Adidas recognised that the jury had reached a mixed decision. "We are pleased that four out of five claims were resolved in our favor, but disappointed by other aspects of the verdict," the company said. "We thank the jurors, the judge, and court staff for their time and service throughout this case. Adidas remains firmly committed to fostering a fair, respectful and inclusive environment for all employees to have an equal opportunity to succeed." The case, filed under docket number 24CV43621, was brought by attorneys Damien Munsinger and Alexis Haskett-Wood of Munsinger Law LLC. Burton's legal team did not respond to requests for comment from CVN after the verdict. Adidas has not yet said whether it plans to appeal the $1.23 million award.You use AI every day. articles.title: Top reasons why people end up in the ER on Thanksgiving — and how to stay safe
articles.summary: With all the slicing, dicing and carving taking place in the kitchen, injuries to the fingers, hands and arms top the list of reasons why people land in the...
articles.body:
The emergency room is the last place anyone wants to end up on Thanksgiving. But the cooking, eating and traveling frenzy surrounding the holiday can introduce exactly the kinds of risks that land some people in the hospital.

"There is usually light volume on Thanksgiving Day, but post-Thanksgiving dinner is when we usually see a surge in the ER," Dr. Poonam Desai , an osteopathic physician who is board-certified in lifestyle medicine and emergency medicine, tells Yahoo.

Dr. Kelly Dougherty , a health care clinical instructor at the Ronald O. Perelman Department of Emergency Medicine at NYU Langone Health, agrees. "As people gather, they spread their germs," she tells Yahoo. "When they head home, they take those germs with them and can develop symptoms of infection, like COVID or influenza, a few days later."

But many patients who rush to the emergency room on Thanksgiving tend to be there due to a holiday-related hazard, notes Dougherty. Overall, Thanksgiving is among the few holidays when ERs actually get fewer visitors than average, according to recent data from Epic Research . But there are exceptions. Here are the top reasons why people land in the ER on turkey day and how to stay out of the hospital over the holiday weekend.

With all the slicing, dicing and carving taking place in the kitchen, injuries to the fingers, hands and arms top the list. "We see a lot of cuts in the ER not only from knives, but also from people slicing their fingers on the lid of a can while opening it," says Dougherty. Hospitals see a sharper spike in lacerations (cuts) than any other Thanksgiving injury, with visits increasing by 26%, Epic Research found.

If you do cut yourself, she says, grab a clean paper towel and apply pressure for 15 to 20 seconds. "Any wounds deeper than a few millimeters might require medical evaluation for stitches and maybe an updated tetanus vaccine," she says.

Burns caused by out-of-control flames in the kitchen are the other top concern. According to the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), Thanksgiving is the peak day for home cooking fires, with more than three times the daily average. In fact, on Thanksgiving Day 2021, an estimated 1,160 home cooking fires were reported to U.S. fire departments — a 297% increase over the daily average. And Epic's study, published in 2026, found that ER visits for burns rise by an average of 18% on Thanksgiving.

If you need to treat a minor first-degree burn , the American Academy of Dermatology Association recommends immediately cooling down the burn site by either immersing the area in cold water or covering it with a cold, wet compress for at least 10 minutes. Then apply petroleum jelly (don't use toothpaste, butter or topical antibiotics) to the burn and cover with a bandage.

"A good way to avoid these types of accidents is to prep in advance so you are not rushing the day of the event," suggests Desai. Also, consider asking others for help (to lighten your load) while also kindly asking your guests to stay out of the kitchen while the chefs are working (to avoid any distractions). Furthermore, refrain from multitasking while chopping carrots, opening a can of cranberry sauce or stirring the turkey gravy on the gas stove. "Be mindful," says Desai.

The American Society for Surgery of the Hand offers turkey-carving safety tips , such as: Carve away from yourself, never toward yourself, and place your free hand opposite the side you're carving toward. Sharpening knives before Thanksgiving can help eliminate the need to carve with force. Also, use an electric knife if you have one to carve the turkey, and cut the bird's bones and joints with kitchen shears instead of a knife.

To prevent house fires, the NFPA stresses the importance of remaining in the kitchen while food is cooking on the stove, as well as checking on the turkey frequently as it cooks in the oven. When frying or sautéing, keep hot oil from splattering and burning skin by gently adding the oil into a pot or pan, followed by slowly increasing the oil's heat until it reaches the desired temperature.

The association also warns against using a turkey fryer that requires cooking oil, since these machines need large amounts of oil at extremely high temperatures.

The most common culprits of stomach pain on Thanksgiving are overindulging and food poisoning. At hospitals, says Desai, doctors may see things like indigestion, which means fullness with a burning sensation after eating; heartburn, also known as acid reflux and involving a burning feeling in the chest or throat; and gastritis, which is inflammation of the stomach lining. Many of the symptoms overlap, such as stomach pain, cramps, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. Burping is another sign of overeating, while a low-grade fever could indicate food poisoning.

"If you happen to eat something that does not agree with you, monitor your symptoms," says Dougherty. "If at any time you are not able to drink water and keep yourself hydrated, you might need a medical evaluation."

And then there's drinking one too many glasses of wine, which can impair both physical and mental abilities. "Alcohol contributes to millions of ER visits a year, and indulging in alcohol puts you at higher risk for any number of injuries that can land you in the ER — falls, head injuries, cuts and fractures," warns Dougherty.

Pace yourself and pay attention to everything you put onto your plate and into your glass. If you suffer from heartburn, consider skipping any dishes that are fried or contain spicy flavorings like chili powder or red pepper, advises Desai. If you're concerned about overdrinking, the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism suggests learning the standard drink sizes so you can count your alcoholic beverages accordingly.

In order to prevent food poisoning , the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises washing your hands, work surfaces and utensils before, during and after preparing foods. Separate raw turkey, chicken, other meats, seafood and eggs from ready-to-eat foods. Use a food thermometer to ensure that poultry and other meats have reached a safe internal temperature . For example, turkey should reach 165 degrees Fahrenheit. And make sure your refrigerator is set at 40°F or below and your freezer at 0°F or below.

What with hosting a big event, grieving loved ones who are no longer here to celebrate, remembering upsetting holidays from the past, dealing with the madness of holiday travel or sitting across the table from a not-so-favorite relative, it's no wonder that Thanksgiving Day can trigger an elevated heart rate.

"The holidays can be a stressful time for many of us, so we tend to have an uptick in stress-related symptoms, such as anxiety and panic attacks," says Desai. She adds that increased stress can exacerbate preexisting mental health conditions, such as depression, as well as physiological ones, such as asthma or chest pain.

According to a 2022 poll conducted by the American Psychiatric Association, 31% of adults reported that they expected to feel more stressed during the upcoming holiday season compared with the previous year.

Begin with making use of a powerful two-letter word. "Say no to gatherings and to people that may make you uncomfortable or contribute to increased stress levels," suggests Desai. She also recommends doing less. "When it comes to the holidays, many people feel they need to do a lot, especially with the pressure of having a social-media-like holiday."

The Anxiety & Depression Association of America advises that you plan and confirm all travel details the day before leaving, avoid overscheduling yourself, refrain from alcohol and drugs and practice stress-reducing techniques, such as slow, deep breathing, meditation and progressive muscle relaxation.

"Thanksgiving is one of the busiest travel times of the year, so there tends to be increased road traffic, sometimes coupled with bad weather, that can lead to increased traffic accidents," says Desai.

The American Automobile Association projects that 55.4 million travelers will head 50 miles or more from home over the 2023 Thanksgiving holiday travel period. The National Safety Council (NSC) estimates that 57,800 injuries from car crashes will require medical attention during the upcoming four-day holiday weekend. In November 2021, 36% of fatalities reported during Thanksgiving travel involved an alcohol-impaired driver.

Whether you're heading to the airport, the train station or someone's home, Desai says you should give yourself plenty of time on the road so you're not worried about being late, which will increase the odds of driving over the speed limit. In its latest press release, AAA reports that INRIX, a provider of transportation data and insights, expects Wednesday, Nov. 22, to be the busiest day on the road during the Thanksgiving travel period, with average travel times as high as 80% over normal in some metro areas. INRIX recommends leaving in the morning or after 6 p.m. to avoid the heaviest holiday congestion.

"Do not drink and drive, and always wear a seat belt," Desai says. The NSC predicts that an estimated 201 lives will be saved this Thanksgiving weekend thanks to seat belts.

Above all, as Dougherty points out, "if you are feeling sick, stay home." She reminds parents with babies that the lungs of infants are vulnerable to RSV , a respiratory virus that infects the lungs and breathing passages. "For those of us non-caretakers who are interacting with infants, be sure to wash your hands and avoid contact with a baby if you're feeling under the weather," she says.

Last but not least, remember not only to bring any medications you'll need while away for Thanksgiving, but also to have an updated list of prescription drugs in your wallet or on your phone on the off chance that you land in the ER.

articles.title: A new lawsuit challenges Trump's changes to the slavery memorial at George Washington's former Philadelphia home, arguing that the stories of nine enslaved people were watered down or removed
articles.summary: A Philadelphia-based history preservation group has sued the Trump administration, accusing it of watering down the history of slavery at the site of
articles.body: A Philadelphia-based history preservation group has sued the Trump administration, accusing it of watering down the history of slavery at the site of former US President George Washington’s home by removing exhibits that documented the experiences of enslaved people.The lawsuit, filed Monday in a federal court in Pennsylvania, names the US Interior Department, Secretary Doug Burgum, the National Park Service (NPS) and its acting director, Jessica Bowron, as defendants.According to the Associated Press (AP), the Avenging the Ancestors Coalition alleges that changes made to the President’s House/Slavery Memorial violate the Fifth Amendment’s equal protection provisions and the Administrative Procedure Act. The latter allows courts to overturn government actions found to be arbitrary, unlawful or an abuse of discretion.Michael Coard, an attorney and founder of the coalition, said the legal action aims to ensure that the complete history of slavery in the US is preserved and presented accurately.Trump administration accused of diluting slavery historyThe memorial, established in 2010, originally documented how nine enslaved people lived in the Philadelphia residence alongside George Washington and his wife, Martha, during the 1790s, when the city served as the US capital.The Trump administration began removing the original exhibit panels earlier this year. The city of Philadelphia challenged the move in court, and a lower court initially ordered the federal government to halt the work in February. However, a federal appeals court overturned that decision on July 3, allowing the changes to proceed.The National Park Service subsequently began installing new interpretive panels at the site.The latest lawsuit claims the replacement displays have diluted the memorial's original message by downplaying the experiences of the nine enslaved people. It alleges that descriptions of the hardships they endured, including physical and sexual violence, have been watered down or removed entirely.The complaint also states that the original glass panels have not been restored and that motion-activated videos at the memorial remain switched off.Lawsuit seeks restoration of original memorialThe Black Journey: African American Walking Tour of Philadelphia has also joined the lawsuit as a plaintiff. The group is seeking the restoration of the memorial to its original condition and a permanent court order preventing the Trump administration from enforcing directives that resulted in the changes.Raina Yancey, who co-founded The Black Journey with her mother, Victoria Ward Yancey, a former park ranger, said the removal of the original displays had taken away an important opportunity to learn about the enslaved people held by Washington.The lawsuit comes amid the Trump administration's wider efforts to roll back diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives across federal agencies and institutions.An executive order signed by Trump in 2025 directed federally owned or controlled historic sites not to display material that "disparage[s] Americans past or living". It also called for exhibits to highlight the achievements and progress of the American people.The Interior Department had defended the revised displays in a statement issued this summer, saying they provided historical context and highlighted significant events at the President's House and other locations within Independence National Historical Park.The department said the panels acknowledged the injustices and contradictions of slavery while highlighting the humanity of the nine enslaved people who lived in Washington's residence.The National Park Service and Interior Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the latest lawsuit. The defendants have 30 days to file their response, according to the plaintiffs' lead counsel, Cara McClellan.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Delhi SIR: Nearly 44 lakh voters may remain off final electoral roll after low Form 6 turnout
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Nearly 44 lakh of the 47.5 lakh voters excluded from Delhi's draft electoral roll may remain out of the final list, with only around 3.5 lakh
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Nearly 44 lakh of the 47.5 lakh voters excluded from Delhi's draft electoral roll may remain out of the final list, with only around 3.5 lakh Form 6 applications received by the end of the claims and objections period on Wednesday, according to officials cited by news agency PTI.A total of 3,31,540 applications were received between August 31 and November 24, officials said, adding that the number was expected to reach around 3.5 lakh by Wednesday.Several of the applications submitted so far were from first-time and new voters.The draft electoral roll, published on August 31, had removed around 47.5 lakh names from Delhi's previous roll of 1.45 crore voters. Of those excluded, 43.32 lakh were categorised as shifted, 2.82 lakh as deceased and 1.45 lakh as duplicate entries.Form 6 is used by citizens, including first-time voters and those whose names are missing from the electoral roll, to apply for inclusion.Fresh effort to trace excluded votersThe low number of applications comes despite a fresh Election Commission exercise to reach voters excluded under the absent, shifted, dead and duplicate (ASDD) categories.These voters, who had been issued enumeration forms during the earlier exercise conducted between June 30 and August 17, were given another opportunity to establish their eligibility and secure a place in the final electoral roll, scheduled to be published on December 22.However, the follow-up exercise has made limited progress. Officials said distribution of enumeration forms began last week, but only a few hundred had been handed out so far. A few voters had also submitted the forms online.Booth-level officers (BLOs) have faced difficulties tracing voters categorised as shifted, particularly tenants who moved out of rented accommodation without leaving their new addresses or contact details.Earlier, a BLO from an unauthorised colony in Babarpur said nearly 300 voters in his polling booth had been placed in the ASDD category, most of them tenants who had vacated their homes.“Most of the people marked under the ASDD category were tenants. They have moved out, but nobody is willing to tell us where they have gone. Even their landlords are unwilling to give anything in writing confirming that the tenants have shifted as they are unaware of their whereabouts,” the BLO said.Form 6, 7 and 8 applicationsBefore the draft roll was published, the office of the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) had received 2,12,400 Form 6 applications up to August 30.During the same period, it received 51,471 Form 7 applications, used to raise objections to the inclusion of names or seek deletion of entries, and 2,60,768 Form 8 applications, which are used for corrections to electoral roll details, including changes of residence.Between August 31 and November 24, another 35,592 Form 7 applications and 1,24,554 Form 8 applications were received.Among Delhi's districts, West recorded the highest number of Form 6 applications during this period, at 40,029. It was followed by North-East with 32,673, South-East with 31,771, North-West with 31,660 and East with 31,619.The distribution and collection of enumeration forms will continue until November 30, while their disposal is scheduled for December 10. The final electoral roll is due to be published on December 22.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi on Wednesday called for public sector undertakings (PSUs) to strengthen their links with Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs)
articles.body: NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi on Wednesday called for public sector undertakings (PSUs) to strengthen their links with Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) for training and recruitment of youth, pitching a ‘Classroom–Company–Career’ approach to bridge the gap between skilling and employment and create job opportunities closer to home, which will help address migration to some extent as well.Chairing the monthly PRAGATI meeting, PM suggested that PSUs should assess their future manpower requirements and partner with ITIs to train and recruit candidates in relevant trades. He also encouraged them to support practical training and apprenticeships and give greater priority to hiring trained ITI graduates.While reviewing the ITI ecosystem and the implementation of PM-SETU, PM Modi called upon chief ministers and chief secretaries to provide leadership in strengthening ITIs and deepening industry participation under PM-SETU. Officials said the PM threw a challenge to chief secretaries to set up five clusters across big states, three in small states and one in UTs in the next three months.Under PM-SETU (Pradhan Mantri Skilling and Employability Transformation through Upgraded ITIs), a “cluster” refers to a group of govt ITIs linked through a hub-and-spoke model, with one major ITI serving as the hub and several smaller ITIs functioning as spokes.Reviewing a power project, PM Modi suggested exploring innovative models for decentralised solar and wind power projects. He said that such projects should be developed closer to centres of consumption wherever feasible, taking into account local resource availability and demand. These efforts should aim to improve the availability of reliable and affordable power and ease pressure on transmission infrastructure.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: SRINAGAR: The J&K government Wednesday said Sheshnag Lake was completely safe and dismissed allegations of construction near the high-altitude lake by the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) that were triggered by a video showing heavy machinery operating near the water body.Forest minister Altaf Kaloo said the earthmover seen in the viral video was operating 200 to 300 feet away from the lake and at a higher elevation. He said not even a grain of soil had entered the lake.The minister, who was scheduled to visit the lake for an on-the-spot inspection on Tuesday, said he could not reach the site due to security concerns. “I had to visit the lake today on the directions of CM Omar Abdullah, but I could not proceed further beyond a certain point as security arrangements were not in place there. Being a protected person, I was advised by the police not to go ahead. I returned and held another detailed meeting with my department,” he said.Kaloo said a 12-member team comprising officials from the departments concerned inspected the area and submitted its findings. “The team reported to me that Sheshnag is completely safe. BRO has not tampered with the track along the lake,” he said.“It is a very holy place for Muslims, Hindus and Sikhs. We respect it, and everybody respects it,” he said.The minister said the BRO was carrying out routine maintenance of the track before and after the annual Amarnath Yatra, including repairing tiles and strengthening its edges, as this work could not be undertaken during the pilgrimage.Kaloo also defended the MOU between the J&K government and the BRO signed early this year under which the organisation was assigned maintenance work of the track.He accused BJP and PDP of politicising the issue ahead of elections in Uttar Pradesh.“There is no track beyond 12 feet of width. The width has to be maintained at 12 feet as per the Supreme Court’s directions. It is meant for pilgrims and horsemen, with six feet for movement in each direction,” he said.PDP‘s Iltija Mufti, however, countered Kaloo, saying that if everything is fine in Sheshnag as claimed by the forest minister, why PDP president Mehbooba Mufti isn’t being allowed to visit the site.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1886, workers began digging from opposite ends of a Wisconsin hill; a year later, they met with an error of barely an inch on one side; the railway tunnel they built has reopened to cyclists after seven years
articles.summary: A railway tunnel built in the 19th century using hand drills, explosives and steam-powered machinery has reopened to cyclists after seven years of closure
articles.body: A railway tunnel built in the 19th century using hand drills, explosives and steam-powered machinery has reopened to cyclists after seven years of closure in Wisconsin. The historic passage, where two construction crews digging from opposite ends of a hill managed to meet with an error of barely an inch, is once again accessible to visitors using the Badger State Trail.According to the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (DNR), which manages the trail and has documented the tunnel's history and restoration, Stewart Tunnel reopened on November 16, 2026. Located just south of Belleville, the tunnel had been closed since 2019 after loose and falling rocks from its ceiling and side walls raised safety concerns. Its reopening follows an extensive rehabilitation project designed to stabilise the ageing structure while retaining its use as a recreational route.How the Stewart Tunnel was built in 1886The history of Stewart Tunnel dates back to December 13, 1886, when the Illinois Central Railroad Company began constructing a railway line between Freeport, Illinois, and Madison, Wisconsin. The tunnel was an important part of this route, which was intended to carry grain, livestock, freight and passengers.Construction began with small teams working simultaneously from the northern and southern ends of the hill. Some workers were local farmers who joined the project to earn additional money during the severe drought of 1887. They initially received $1.25 per day, while basic accommodation near the construction site cost $3.50 per week. The planned tunnel was approximately a quarter of a mile long, with a curved passage measuring 21 feet high and 14 feet wide. Building it required considerable manual effort and machinery that was relatively advanced for the period.Workers used hand drills to make holes in the limestone before placing explosives to break up the rock. At the northern entrance, a hoisting apparatus helped remove excavated material, while steam shovels were subsequently brought in to speed up the work. A 48-ton steam shovel operated at the northern end, while a smaller 20-ton machine was used at the southern end.The southern crew also used a small locomotive called Stella to transport excavated rock to a dumping area known as Lynn Hollow. Later, compressed-air drills replaced the steam-operated drills to improve the pace of excavation. The work was not without difficulties. In September 1887, workers went on strike demanding higher wages, and many left the project. Their daily pay was subsequently increased to $1.75. The crews also encountered a large underground stream and an unstable roof, forcing them to suspend drilling for several days while the structure was supported.The two teams finally met in December 1887. According to the Wisconsin DNR's historical account, the alignment was remarkably accurate: one side was off by about an inch and the other by less than three-quarters of an inch. The tunnel was named after James Stewart, the Pennsylvania contractor who died after being thrown from a buggy while surveying the proposed railway route.From railway passage to recreational trailThe tunnel initially served the Illinois Central Railroad, carrying passenger and freight trains through the region. Passenger services continued until the 1960s, while freight trains operated until 1976. As railway use declined, the corridor eventually became part of a recreational trail. The Wisconsin DNR began exploring its conversion in 1997, and the Badger State Trail's master plan was approved in 2006. The trail now extends approximately 40 miles between Madison and the Wisconsin-Illinois border, passing through farmland, woodland, meadows and several small communities.Stewart Tunnel became one of its distinctive attractions because of its curved design. Unlike a straight tunnel, visitors entering the passage cannot immediately see its other end. However, falling limestone created a safety problem. In September 2019, the DNR closed the tunnel after rocks dislodged from its ceiling and landed on the trail. A temporary route along Tunnel Road allowed cyclists, hikers and other trail users to bypass the passage.What changed during the restorationThe rehabilitation involved installing a corrugated metal liner inside the approximately 1,200-foot-long tunnel. The DNR selected this approach after considering an engineering review by GEI Consultants that examined nine alternatives and receiving 901 public comments during a consultation period in 2022. According to a November 22, 2026 report by New Glarus 360, the restoration required more than 317,100 pounds of steel liner plates, over 65,000 nuts and bolts, and 4,610 cubic yards of cellular grout. Crews also installed drainage systems, footings and bulkheads, with concrete pumped around and over the new structure.The design was intended to protect visitors from falling rocks while preserving the tunnel's importance as a winter habitat for hibernating bats. Space was retained above the metal lining to accommodate the bats. The DNR confirmed that Stewart Tunnel reopened on November 16, 2026, allowing visitors to use the passage again after seven years of detours. However, the work is not entirely finished. The department plans another temporary closure of approximately one month in spring 2027 to address an area near the southern entrance, complete minor grading and drainage work, and upgrade the permanent gates.The reopening restores access to a landmark that has served different generations of travellers, from 19th-century railway passengers to today's cyclists and hikers.You use AI every day.
